problem_data.story:
A district simply vanished on the night of March 15th.

A delivery driver named Sofia Stone was the first to report it. She had been rushing south along Highway 7 through the Pearlbrook Region, trying to make up time after a longer-than-expected stop at a distribution center, when she slammed on her brakes. If she'd gone another thirty feet, she would have driven straight into the void where the highway should have continued.

Sofia couldn't see the full extent of the emptiness because of the darkness, but it looked massive. Bigger than any sinkhole she'd ever heard of. Her first thought was some kind of catastrophic infrastructure collapse. She reversed two hundred feet, set out emergency flares, then sped off to find a phone signal.

State authorities converged on the site from multiple directions. Communicating by radio across the vast emptiness, they confirmed that an entire district was definitely missing from the heart of the region. They called in the National Guard.

The Guard surrounded the area with personnel—more than eight hundred were needed—to keep people from falling into the void. A helicopter pilot who flew over it reported that it looked as if someone had used a giant cookie cutter on the landscape, removing a perfect section from Pearlbrook's interior.

The regional transit authority complained that one of its automated trains was missing. The train's schedule had it passing through the area at 11:47 PM. That seemed to fix the time of the disappearance around midnight.

Someone pointed out that March 15th was the Ides of March, historically a day of upheaval.

Somebody else said they'd better check for radiation or chemical contamination. An environmental safety official brought detection equipment, but everything registered normal.

A National Guard officer volunteered to take a vehicle down into the void, having found what seemed like a navigable slope. She was gone for over an hour, but when she emerged on the other side, she reported that the void was smooth, bowl-shaped, and showed no signs of explosion or fire. She'd found no people, no buildings—no trace of anything except the void itself.

The Governor asked federal authorities whether any unidentified aircraft had been in the region. Washington said no. The Department of Defense and various agencies denied conducting any secret experiments.

Nor had there been any sensitive facilities in the missing district that might have been targeted. The area's biggest employer was a film production studio, and the second-biggest was a venture capital firm specializing in virtual reality startups.

A commercial pilot found the missing district early on the morning of March 16th. The pilot, Captain Jonathan Spencer, who prided himself on rational thinking and logic, was afraid he was seeing something impossible. The object emerged from a cloud layer at fifteen thousand feet, and Spencer changed course to avoid it. He noted with minimal relief that his co-pilot also saw the thing and wondered why it wasn't moving.

Then he saw the broadcast tower on it.

A few minutes later, he had relayed a message from the floating landmass, addressed to anyone listening:

It said that the district had declared independence from the ground.

One other radio message came from the airborne territory on that first day. An amateur radio operator reported an unidentified voice saying plaintively:

"Getting cold up here!"

Kevin Mason had been dozing in the observation car of the express train when it jerked to a stop. He looked out the window, hoping this was Magnolia Province, where he planned to catch a connecting flight. But it wasn't. All he could see were emergency lights moving along the tracks.

The conductor looked into the car. A woman with striking auburn hair across the aisle—Kevin had noticed her earlier—asked, "Why did we stop?"

"Someone flagged us down," the conductor said. "We don't normally stop here on the Pearlbrook route."

The woman's hair was professionally styled, and Kevin had observed earlier that she carried herself with the confidence of someone used to authority. Her eyes had been focused on a tablet when Kevin entered the car, giving him time to notice her sharp features and the slight frown lines that suggested she was accustomed to finding fault. Her expression was one of practiced skepticism.

If the woman had given Kevin more than a cursory glance, she would have seen a man in his late twenties—about her age—lean and athletic, with dark hair, an unremarkable face, and a habit of tapping his fingers thoughtfully when concentrating.

But likely all she noticed was the locked metal case he carried, secured by a biometric lock to his left wrist.

"Will we be here long?" Kevin asked the conductor. He didn't want to miss his flight. The sooner he got to Highpoint Territory, the sooner he'd deliver the case. The biometric lock was one reason why his interest in the auburn-haired woman had been only passing.

"Can't say," the conductor told him. He let the door close and went down to the tracks.

Kevin hesitated, shrugged at the woman, said, "Excuse me," and followed the conductor. About twenty people were milling around the train as it sat in the dark. Kevin made his way forward and found a larger group gathered ahead of the locomotive.

Some kind of barricade had been erected across the tracks, covered with every imaginable warning device. There were LED flares, reflective barriers, emergency lights, and even an orange safety vest.

Kevin saw two people who must have been the engineer and assistant talking to an older woman wearing a civil defense vest, a long coat, and hiking boots.

"You'd go over the edge, I'm telling you," the older woman was saying.

"If you don't clear this obstruction," the engineer said, "I'll push right through it. Over the edge? Are you serious?"

"See for yourself," the woman in the vest said. "Go ahead. Look."

The engineer was exasperated. She turned to her assistant. "You look. Humor her. Then let's go."

The woman—she introduced herself as Dr. Vanessa Shaw—went off with the assistant. Kevin followed them. They had walked a quarter mile along the gravel when the assistant stopped. "Okay," she said, "where's this edge? I don't see anything." The tracks seemed to stretch endlessly into the darkness.

"It's another half mile or so," Dr. Shaw said.

"Well, let's hurry. We haven't got all night."

The older woman chuckled. "I'm afraid you do."

They came to it at last, stopping well back from it. Dr. Shaw seemed almost proud as she made a theatrical gesture.

"Behold," she said. "The edge of our new world."

True enough, everything seemed to stop, and they could see lights from the ground shining far below where ground should not be visible.

Kevin Mason and the assistant walked cautiously toward the edge while Dr. Shaw strode ahead with the confidence of someone who had been there before. But there was a wind, and they didn't venture too close. Nevertheless, Kevin could see that it was apparently a clean, precise edge, not ragged like something caused by an explosion. This had the feeling of intentional design.

Standing on tiptoe and fighting a wave of vertigo, Kevin looked over the edge. He didn't need to stand on tiptoe any more than he needed to grip the armrest during a tense movie scene, but the situation seemed to demand it. Over the edge, he could see a vast section of the Pearlbrook Region spread out below. At least he assumed it was Pearlbrook—from up here, the entire region was visible, surrounding the void where they had once been connected to it.

Kevin looked at the assistant, who had a stunned expression, then at Dr. Shaw, who was smiling and nodding.

"You see what I mean," she said. "You would have gone right over. I believe it's a three-mile drop back to Pearlbrook below."

"Of course you could have stayed on the train," the man driving the electric sedan said, "but I really think you'll be more comfortable at the Institute."

Kevin Mason, sitting in the back seat with the auburn-haired woman from the observation car, asked, "Institute?"

"The Institute for Advanced Studies. We focus on applied ethics and cultural sociology, though we're not traditionally accredited. What did you say your name was, miss?"

"Sasha Holmes," she said. "I work in international diplomacy."

"Ms. Holmes. I'm Jin Gupta. You know Mr. Mason, I suppose."

The woman smiled slightly. "We've exchanged glances." Kevin nodded and smiled back.

"There's plenty of room in the guest quarters," Jin said. "People don't exactly line up to visit the Institute."

"Are you connected with it?" Kevin asked.

"Me? No. I'm the district administrator. The whole place has really risen in the world, hasn't it?"

"Literally overnight," Sasha Holmes said. "If what Mr. Mason and the train assistant say is true. I haven't seen the edge myself."

"You'll have a better chance to look in the morning," the administrator said, "assuming we don't settle back down in the meantime."

"Was there any kind of explosion?" Kevin asked.

"No. There wasn't any sensation at all, as far as I noticed. I was reviewing some strategic planning documents on my tablet—we're always dealing with community organizing issues here. Well, suddenly my internet connection improved dramatically. Then the phone rang, and it was Dr. Shaw."

"The older woman with the vest and the hiking boots?" Sasha Holmes asked.

"Yes. Vanessa Shaw, Director of the Institute's Applied Physics program."

"Applied Physics?" Kevin asked.

"Among other things. The Institute isn't bound by traditional academic constraints. Well, Dr. Shaw called and said, 'Jin'—that's my name—'we've achieved separation.' She was being cryptic, of course. I said, 'What?' and then she explained."

"Explained what?" Sasha Holmes asked. "I mean, does she have any theory about this?"

"She has theories about everything. I think what she was trying to convey was that this—this levitation—confirmed her gravitational manipulation hypothesis."

"What's that?" Kevin asked.

"I haven't the faintest idea. I'm an administrator, not a physicist. Dr. Shaw went on about it for a while, something about artificial gravity fields and quantum mechanics, but I think she was mainly calling as a courtesy, so I wouldn't look foolish the next morning."

"What's the population here?" Kevin asked.

"Four thousand, including the Institute staff and students. Four thousand and fifty-three, counting you people from the train. I guess you'll be with us for a while."

"What do you mean by that?" Sasha Holmes asked sharply.

"Well, I don't see how you can get down. Do you?"

"Does this district have an airport?" Kevin asked. "I need to get to Highpoint Territory."

"Nope," Jin said. "No airport. No suitable landing area, either."

"Maybe not for planes," Kevin said, "but helicopters could land almost anywhere."

"No helicopters here."

"Maybe not. But I bet they'll be swarming around by morning."

"Hm," said Jin Gupta. Kevin couldn't quite read his expression in the rearview mirror. "I suppose they could. Well, here's the Institute. You go right through that entrance, where the others are going. There's Dr. Shaw. I need to speak with her—excuse me."

The administrator hurried off across the campus. Kevin looked at Sasha Holmes, who was frowning. "Are you thinking," he asked, "that Administrator Gupta was perhaps less than completely forthcoming?"

"I'm thinking," she said, "that I should have stayed at my conference another day and taken a direct flight."

"Where were you headed?" Kevin asked.

"Highpoint Territory. I work with the diplomatic corps." She paused. "What do you do, Mr. Mason?"

"I'm a courier for a tech company. Artificial intelligence prototypes, mostly. Hence the locked case."

"I see," she said, though her tone suggested she wasn't entirely convinced. "We should find somewhere to sleep. It's getting late."

"Agreed," Kevin said. They were met by a middle-aged man who introduced himself as Marco Watson, the Institute's hospitality coordinator. "We'll make you comfortable," he said. "What a night! Dr. Shaw is absolutely thrilled. We haven't had this much excitement since the particle accelerator malfunctioned."

They caught a glimpse of Dr. Shaw, still in her civil defense vest, gesturing animatedly to someone in a lab coat.

Kevin Mason had slept, but not well. He'd tried to maneuver the metal case through his sleeve to remove his jacket, but whatever was inside was too large. The Institute had given him a private room in the guest quarters, and he'd removed his pants but had to sleep in his shirt and jacket. He got up feeling grimy and did what minimal preparation was possible.

It was eight o'clock according to his watch, and activity was evident outside. He had a view of the campus from his window. Bright sun illuminated young people moving generally toward a low building—probably the cafeteria—while others moved in various directions. The air was remarkably clear, and the morning shadows were sharp. Only then did he fully remember that he and the entire district were suspended in the air, three miles above the region below.

He went through the guest quarters. A few people were still sleeping. Others had left their unmade beds. He shivered as he stepped outside. It was cold, though not freezing, and his breath was visible. First he'd eat, he decided, so he'd have energy to examine the edge in daylight and see the ground below.

The dining hall was cafeteria-style, and he got in line with a tray for juice, eggs, and coffee. He saw no one he knew, but as he looked for a table, a slender woman with platinum blonde hair smiled and gestured to the empty seat across from her.

"You're Mr. Mason," she said. "Won't you join me?"

"Thanks," he said, unloading his tray. "How did you know?"

"The mystery man with the locked case. You're hard to miss. I'm Nathan Morris—yes, Nathan, not Natalie. My parents had a sense of humor. Are you with some intelligence agency? Or did you steal something valuable?"

"How do you do. No, just a tech courier. What an unusual name. Dr. Shaw's student?"

"Assistant, actually," she said. "Also her daughter, though we keep that quiet professionally. A pity, because if I'd had a choice, I'd have gone to a normal university. As it is, I'm duty-bound to represent the second generation at the experimental facility."

"Experimental facility? You mean the Institute?" Kevin struggled to manipulate his utensils without knocking things over with his attached case.

"Here, let me help you," Nathan said, cutting his food. "You should order scrambled eggs tomorrow. Yes, the Institute. Home of the unorthodox theory and the controversial experiment."

"I'm sure it's not that bad. Thanks. As for tomorrow, I hope to be gone by then."

"How do you plan to leave? Float down on a parachute?"

"I'll find a way. I'm more interested in how I got up here."

"You were levitated, like everyone else."

"You make it sound deliberate, Ms. Morris, as if someone lifted an entire district for some purpose."

"Well, that's debatable. Have you seen the news feeds?"

"I didn't know there were any."

"Actually, there's just one local outlet. This is a special edition. The editor must have worked all night." She pulled out her phone and showed him a digital edition.

Kevin blinked at the headline: "District Gets High"

"The editor's something of an independent thinker, like most people around here," Nathan said.

Kevin read the story, which seemed to treat the situation with surprising levity despite its gravity.

"Residents planning to travel beyond district boundaries today are advised to reconsider. It's a long way down. Where we were once surrounded by Pearlbrook, today our territory ends literally at the district line.

A Citizens' Emergency Barrier Committee is being organized, but in the meantime, everyone is warned to stay well away from the edge. The laws of physics seem to have been suspended for the district, but it's doubtful the same exemption would apply to a curious individual bent on investigating..."

Kevin skimmed the rest. "I don't see anything about it being deliberate."

Nathan had been preparing Kevin's coffee. She pushed it toward him and said, "It's not on the front page. The editor and Administrator Gupta don't get along, so you'll find the administrator's statement in a box on page three."

Kevin navigated to the page, took a sip of coffee, nodded his thanks, and read:

"Administrator Claims Independence from Ground

Administrator Jin Gupta, in a proclamation issued locally and transmitted to Pearlbrook via drone, announced today that our district has declared independence. His reasons were as vague as his explanation.

The 'reasons' include: (1) we have been neglected by regional and federal agencies; (2) the Institute has been ridiculed by traditional academic institutions; and (3) we have been subject to unfair pollution control regulations that hampered the film production industry.

The 'explanation' consists of a 73-page paper on gravitational field manipulation by Dr. Vanessa Shaw of the Institute, which the editor (a) does not fully understand; (b) lacks space to publish; and which (being highly technical) he (c) cannot adequately summarize for general readers."

Kevin said, "I'm beginning to like this editor."

"He's wonderful," Nathan said. "He's about the only one in town who challenges Mother."

"Does your mother claim that she levitated the whole district off the ground?"

"Not to me. I'm one of those inconveniences, a skeptic. She gave up trying to convince me when I was seventeen. I had a physics professor at a summer program—not at the Institute—who gave me all kinds of difficult questions to ask Mother. I asked them, being naturally contrary, and Mother has considered me intellectually lost ever since."

"How old are you, Ms. Morris, if I may ask?"

She sat up straighter, adjusting her sweater. She had an excellent figure, intelligent eyes, a delicate nose, and expressive lips. She could have been the star of any campus with a more conventional student body.

"You may call me Nathan," she said. "And I'm twenty-two."

Kevin grinned. "Recently?"

"Four months ago. How old are you, Mr. Mason?"

"Kevin's the name I've had for twenty-eight years. Please use it."

"Gladly. And now, Kevin, unless you want more coffee, I'll accompany you to the edge of the world."

"On such short notice?" Kevin was intrigued. Last night the woman from the train had been coolly professional, and this morning a friendly blonde was apparently offering companionship. He wondered briefly where Sasha Holmes was.

"I'll admit to the double meaning," Nathan said. "What I meant—for now—was that we can walk out to where we used to be connected to the rest of Pearlbrook and see how the ground is managing without us."

"I'd like that. But don't you have work to do?"

"Sure. I'm supposed to be analyzing data from yesterday's sensors. But I'm an expert procrastinator, which is why I'm still finishing my graduate work at my advanced age. On to the edge!"

They walked south from the campus and came to the train tracks. The train was still there, going nowhere. It had been abandoned except for the conductor, who had dutifully remained aboard overnight.

"What's happening?" he asked when he saw them. "Any word from Pearlbrook below?"

"Not that I know of," Kevin said. He introduced Nathan Morris. "What are you going to do?"

"What can I do?" the conductor asked.

"You can go to the Institute and have breakfast," Nathan said. "Nobody's going to bother your train."

The conductor decided that sounded reasonable and left.

"You know," Kevin said, "before the train stopped last night, I thought I saw a stream running alongside the tracks."

"Clearwater Stream," Nathan said. "That's right. It's just over there."

"Is it still there? Hasn't it all poured off the edge by now? Was that our water supply?"

Nathan shrugged. "All I know is the water still works. Let's check the stream."

They found it flowing normally between its banks.

"Looks the same," she said.

"That's strange. Come on, let's follow it to the edge."

The edge, as Nathan called it, looked even more dramatic in daylight. Everything simply stopped. There was a residential area with houses and yards, then nothing. There was Clearwater Stream flowing along, then nothing. In the distance, a grove of trees simply ended.

"Where is the water going?" Kevin asked. "I can't tell."

"Down to the region below, presumably. Rain for the people down there."

"But it should be drained by now. I'm going to look."

"Don't! You'll fall!"

"I'll be careful." He walked cautiously toward the edge. Nathan followed, a few feet behind. He stopped a yard from the brink and waited for vertigo to pass. The Pearlbrook Region was spread out like a satellite image, far below. Kevin took another careful step, then sat down.

"Careful," said Nathan. She laughed nervously, then sat down too.

"I still can't see where the water goes," Kevin said. He lay flat on his stomach and began to inch forward. "You stay there."

Finally, he inched to a point where, by stretching, he could almost reach the edge. He gave another push forward and his right hand closed over the brink. For a moment he lay there, breathing hard, head pressed to the ground.

"How do you feel?" Nathan asked.

"Terrified. When I get my nerve back, I'll lift my head and look."

Nathan reached out tentatively, then firmly grasped his ankle. "Just in case of wind," she said.

"Thanks. That helps. Okay, here goes." He lifted his head. "Damn."

"What?"

"It's still not clear. Do you have a mirror?"

"I have a compact." She took it from her bag with her free hand and tossed it to him. It rolled and Kevin had to grab to keep it from going over. Nathan gasped. Kevin was momentarily shaken and had to put his head back down. "Sorry," she said.

Kevin opened the compact and carefully transferred it to his right hand. He held it out beyond the edge and peered into it, focusing on the end of the stream. "Now I see it. The water isn't going off the edge!"

"It isn't? Then where?"

"Down, yes, but it's as if it's going into a vertical shaft, just short of the edge."

"Why? How?"

"I can't see clearly, but that's what it looks like. Hold on. I'm coming back." He inched away from the edge, then stood and brushed himself off. He returned her compact. "I think we need to check the other end of the stream."

"The source?"

"Exactly."

Clearwater Stream didn't cut through the center of the district but flowed in an arc through the southern part. They had about two miles to walk, past Clearwater Bridge—which used to connect to the surrounding region, Nathan said—past the Recreation Center, and on to the edge again.

But as they approached what should be the source of the stream, they found a chain-link fence blocking the area. "This is new," Nathan said.

The fence, which had a sign on it reading "WARNING—ELECTRIFIED," was semicircular, with each end at the edge, and tarps hung behind it so they couldn't see the mouth of the stream. The water flowed from under the tarp and fence.

"Look how it comes in pulses," Nathan said.

"As if it's being pumped."

Kevin studied the warning sign more carefully. Smaller text below the main warning read: "Protecting water source infrastructure. Electrical charge sufficient to cause serious injury."

"What's the other water source?" Kevin asked.

"North Reservoir, probably," Nathan said. "It's used for the water treatment facility."

"Is the reservoir entirely within the district boundaries?"

"I don't know."

"If it were on the edge, and if someone took a boat out on it, I wonder what would happen?"

"I know one thing—I wouldn't be there holding your ankle while you found out."

She took his arm as they gazed past the electrified fence at the surrounding region below and to the west.

"It's impressive, isn't it?" she said. "I wonder if that's Magnolia Province way over there?"

He patted her hand absent-mindedly. "I wonder if it's west at all. I mean, how do we know we're maintaining the same orientation as before?"

"We could tell by the sun, silly."

"Of course," he said, grinning. "And I guess we're not high enough to see very far. If we were, we'd be able to see the mountain ranges."

They were contemplating the geography when a plane emerged from a cloud layer and, a moment later, veered sharply. They could make out commercial airline markings on the fuselage. As it turned, they imagined they could see faces at the windows. They waved and thought they saw people wave back. Then the plane climbed eastward and disappeared.

"Well," Kevin said as they turned back toward the Institute, "now we know they know. Maybe we'll start getting some answers. Or, if not answers, then rescue."

"Rescue?" Nathan squeezed the arm she was holding. "Why? You'd rather be down there in Pearlbrook than up here with me?"

"If you mean don't I like you, the answer is yes, I do. But if I don't get out of this biometric lock soon so I can shower and change clothes, you're not going to like me."

"You're still quite presentable, if a bit scruffy." She stopped, still holding his arm, and he turned so they were face to face. "So kiss me," she said, "before you get any worse."

They were in the middle of an extremely pleasant kiss when the metal case at the end of Kevin's biometric lock began to emit a high-pitched alarm.

Later that evening, after the alarm had been silenced and Kevin had been questioned extensively by Marco Watson about the case's contents, he found himself alone in the Institute's small library. He had been searching for maps of the region, hoping to understand exactly where the district boundaries lay.

In a dusty corner, he discovered a shelf of bound municipal records. He pulled out a volume labeled "District Charter and Founding Documents" and began leafing through it.

The opening page featured an ornate certificate with an elaborate border and several official seals. The date was 1952, and signatures of the original trustees filled the bottom half of the page. Much of the text was faded, but Kevin could make out references to "the Pearlbrook Region" and "independent governance."

Kevin kept reading. A section on "District Boundaries" included surveyor's notes describing the perimeter in relation to the surrounding Pearlbrook townships. The notes referenced landmarks: "northern boundary at the ridge crest," "southern boundary at Pearl Creek," "eastern boundary following the old logging road."

He turned to a chapter on public utilities. The founding documents established municipal services to manage water, electricity, and waste removal. A footnote explained that all municipal equipment would bear the district seal and identification marks.

A collection of old photographs lined one wall of the library. Kevin studied them—founding members of the Institute, dedication ceremonies, early construction. One showed a group standing before a stone marker at what appeared to be the district's main entrance. The marker's inscription was too small to read in the photograph, but Kevin could see it featured the same tree-and-ridge symbol he'd noticed on various buildings.

He pulled out his phone and searched through the cached version of the local newspaper he'd read that morning. In the classified section, buried among notices for lost pets and furniture sales, he found an advertisement: "Historical Society Annual Meeting, Thursday 7 PM at the Community Center. This year's topic: 'Our Unique Identity Within Greater Pearlbrook.'"

Through the window, he could see the lights of the small downtown area—four thousand people, the administrator had said, now suspended three miles above the region they had once called home. Four thousand people who, if the administrator's proclamation was to be believed, had no intention of returning to their place within Pearlbrook.

Kevin wondered how many of them had chosen this. How many had even known it was coming.

The next morning, Kevin walked through the downtown area before breakfast, wanting to see more of the community whose fate he now shared. The main street was lined with small shops and businesses, most displaying a consistent visual identity—a stylized oak tree with roots extending downward into a ridge-like formation.

He passed a coffee shop called "Ridge Roasters" and a bookstore with "Oak & Page" on its awning. A real estate office had a faded sign in the window: "Welcome to Our Ridge-Top Community."

At the corner, a bronze plaque mounted on a lamppost caught his attention. It commemorated the district's founding and included a brief history: the area had been carved out of Pearlbrook in 1952, established by a group of academics and entrepreneurs who wanted to create an independent research community. Kevin noted how the plaque repeatedly emphasized the district's separation from "the surrounding Pearlbrook townships."

Kevin made his way to the public library next, a small building near the town square. The librarian, an elderly woman with reading glasses perched on her nose, looked up as he entered.

"You're one of the train passengers," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Kevin Mason. I'm trying to learn more about where I've ended up."

"Temporarily ended up, I hope. For your sake, anyway. Some of us chose to live here. I'm Margaret Chen—I've been the librarian for thirty years." She gestured at the shelves around her. "What would you like to know?"

"The basics, I suppose. When was this place established? How did it come to be separate from the rest of Pearlbrook?"

Margaret smiled and pulled out a worn pamphlet. "We published this for our fiftieth anniversary. Take it—we have boxes of them." The cover showed the familiar oak-and-ridge emblem.

Kevin flipped through it. The pamphlet's text was careful to always distinguish "our district" from "the Pearlbrook Region," but he noticed the actual district name appeared only in abbreviated form throughout—"O.R. District"—as if the full name were so well-known to residents that spelling it out would be redundant.

"A common misconception among outsiders," Margaret continued, "is that we're part of Pearlbrook. We've always been separate—administratively, at least. The district was incorporated in 1952 as an independent entity. The founders wanted autonomy for their research institute without interference from regional politics."

"But you're surrounded by Pearlbrook on all sides. Or you were."

"Geography and governance aren't the same thing. We've always been our own district, with our own administration, our own utilities. Pearlbrook is just what surrounds us. Or surrounded us, I suppose I should say now."

Kevin thanked her and wandered through the stacks. In the local history section, he found a slim volume with a water-damaged cover. The title was partially obscured, but he could read "...History of Our Independent District: 1952-2000." The author was listed as a former Institute professor.

He skimmed the introduction, which described the founders' vision of creating a self-governing research community that could operate independently of regional bureaucracy. The second chapter discussed the naming of the district, but the key pages had suffered water damage and were illegible. What Kevin could read mentioned "the prominent geological feature along the northern boundary" and "the dominant tree species of the original forest."

On his way back to the Institute, Kevin passed the town hall. A bronze seal was mounted beside the entrance, showing the same oak-and-ridge design he'd seen throughout town. The seal's outer ring contained text, but decades of weather had worn the lettering smooth in places. He could make out "...ISTRICT OF..." and what might have been "...ARLBROOK REGION" beneath it—or possibly "...RIDGE" followed by something else. The corrosion made it impossible to be certain.

He was still thinking about what he'd learned when he encountered Sasha Holmes outside the Institute's main building.

"Mr. Mason," she said. "You've been exploring."

"Getting my bearings. Have you?"

"In a manner of speaking. I've been monitoring communications with the ground." She paused. "The regional authorities in Pearlbrook are demanding our return. They're calling it an act of terrorism."

"Interesting phrasing—'our return.' As if we belong to them."

"Mm. The administrator disagrees. He says the district has exercised its right to self-determination. He keeps emphasizing that this area was never actually part of Pearlbrook—just surrounded by it."

"Does a district have that right? To simply... leave?"

Sasha's expression was unreadable. "That's a question for diplomats and lawyers. What I can tell you is that Washington is taking this seriously. They've scrambled aircraft and are establishing a no-fly zone around us."

"Around us? We're three miles up. That's quite a zone."

"Indeed." She studied him for a moment. "You seem to have learned something on your walk. Care to share?"

Kevin considered. "Just that there's a lot of local pride here about not being Pearlbrook. Every sign, every emblem—it all emphasizes the distinction. But I still haven't figured out what this place is actually called. Everyone just says 'the district' or 'our community.'"

"The locals know what they call it. They don't need to keep reminding each other."

"True. The pamphlets use 'O.R. District.' I assume that stands for something."

Sasha nodded slowly. "The news broadcasts from below keep referring to 'the missing Pearlbrook district.' The Pearlbrook authorities seem to consider this area part of their region."

"But the residents here disagree. Strongly, apparently."

"Strong enough to levitate three miles into the air to make the point."

"Perhaps we should find out together," Kevin said. "What this place is actually called, I mean. And whether anyone here besides Dr. Shaw knew this was coming."

Sasha offered a slight smile. "After breakfast?"

Kevin nodded, and they walked toward the dining hall. Behind them, the broadcast tower that Captain Spencer had spotted from his aircraft blinked its red warning lights against the morning sky, marking the position of the floating district for any aircraft that might approach.

And far below, in the void where the district had once rested, the residents of Pearlbrook looked up at the impossible sight and argued about what to call the thing that had left them behind.
problem_data.story_title: And Then the Town Took Off
problem_data.question: What was the name of the district that vanished?

turns.speaker: dishonest
